cells.quote: Across reviews, immersive technologies were reported as potentially beneficial for short-term communication performance, learner engagement, and perceived confidence, particularly in comparison with no intervention or some traditional teaching formats.
cells.note: The umbrella review included heterogeneous systematic reviews and primary studies, including studies without comparison groups; findings were interpreted cautiously because all included reviews were rated critically low in methodological quality.

cells.quote: Jensen et al. [18] reported advantages over no intervention or traditional teaching methods, but no clear superiority over non-technology-based simulations approaches; moreover, students frequently perceived VPs as lacking realism.
cells.note: The finding is reported across a systematic review and concerns short-term or immediate communication outcomes; the text does not report a pooled effect size.

cells.quote: Cho and Kim [20] identified a moderate effect in favor of VR/AR compared with traditional formats, although heterogeneity was high.
cells.note: The study text reports the effect qualitatively as moderate but does not provide a numerical effect estimate.

cells.quote: Across reviews, immersive technologies were reported as potentially beneficial for short-term communication performance, learner engagement, and perceived confidence, particularly in comparison with no intervention or some traditional teaching formats.
cells.note: Engagement and confidence were reported as perceived or short-term outcomes; the review-level evidence was heterogeneous and methodologically critically low.

D.treatment: topics selected by UM students in Round 1
D.comparison: topics selected only by educators in Round 1

O.outcome_detail: Round 2 mean priority score for topics to be developed into e-learning objects

cells.quote: For UM in Round 1, there was a difference in the topics selected by the students and educators. In Round 2, the students gave a higher mean score (Round 2) to the topics selected by themselves compared to those selected only by the educators (Fig 2A).
cells.note: The study reports mean-score differences but no printed effect size.
